name: PGM Extra (pgm-extra-rs)
workload: Point-query and range-query benchmark over 1M random u64 keys (10K queries), comparing PGM-index variants (epsilon=16/64/256) against Rust's BTreeSet/BTreeMap and HashMap on an Apple M1 Pro
claimed_speedup: PGM (eps=256) 1.7x faster point queries than BTreeSet (489.5us vs 851.6us), 3.2x smaller memory (7.7MB vs 25.0MB), range-scan 1.4x faster (verbatim from README benchmark tables)
tradeoffs: PGM must rebuild segments on mutation, so it favors read-mostly workloads; main claimed win is 2.7-3.2x smaller memory footprint alongside 1.3-1.7x faster point lookups than BTreeSet/BTreeMap.
caveats: First-party micro-benchmark; no compiler flags stated, single machine (Apple M1 Pro), not independently reproduced. This is a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of the PGM-index idea, not a fork of the canonical gvinciguerra/PGM-index (already catalogued).

name: PGM++ (adaptive search-strategy PGM-index)
workload: Equality lookup benchmark (SOSD-style) comparing a mixture of search strategies with auto-tuned hyper-parameters against the original PGM-index and other learned indexes at comparable space cost
claimed_speedup: up to 2.31x vs original PGM-Index and 1.56x vs state-of-the-art learned indexes at comparable space cost (per arXiv abstract)
tradeoffs: Requires a calibrated cost model to pick a search-strategy mixture per dataset, adding tuning complexity over PGM's plain binary/linear search.
caveats: Paper only (arXiv:2410.00846, 'Why Are Learned Indexes So Effective but Sometimes Ineffective?'); searched GitHub for 'PGM++' and found no matching repository. Numbers taken from the abstract only; hardware/compiler unstated. Not the same repo as gvinciguerra/Learned-indexes-effectiveness (an earlier, different paper by the same PGM-index author).
found_via: arXiv API: search_query=abs:"learned index" AND abs:"B-tree", sortBy=submittedDate

name: MountDB (learned indexing integrated into RocksDB)
workload: Read/write throughput after deploying specialized learned indexes at RocksDB's Memtable and on-disk-file levels, with a model-reuse mechanism across Memtable instances
claimed_speedup: up to 1.5x higher write throughput and 2.1x higher read throughput vs state-of-the-art systems (per arXiv abstract)
tradeoffs: Requires modifying RocksDB internals (Memtable and on-disk index replacement) and maintaining model-reuse state across Memtable instances.
caveats: Paper only ('A Pragmatic Approach to Learned Indexing in RocksDB'); no GitHub repo found, searched 'MountDB' with no match. 'state-of-the-art systems' baseline is ambiguous about whether it means stock RocksDB or a competing learned-index system; numbers from abstract only.
found_via: arXiv API: search_query=abs:"learned index" AND abs:"B-tree", sortBy=submittedDate

name: SNKV
workload: 1M records on Linux; sequential writes, random reads, sequential scan, random updates/deletes, and mixed workload, comparing SNKV (talks directly to SQLite's B-tree engine, skipping the SQL layer) against SQLite itself. Both use WAL mode, synchronous=NORMAL, 8MB cache, 4KB pages; SQLite uses a WITHOUT ROWID table.
claimed_speedup: 1.64x sequential writes, 1.77x random reads, 1.85x sequential scan, 1.9x random updates, ~2x random deletes, 1.79x mixed workload (verbatim from README benchmark table)
hardware: unspecified Linux machine (no CPU model stated)
tradeoffs: Skips SQL layer entirely (no parser/query planner/VDBE), so loses SQL query capability; gains native TTL, encryption, column families and an optional HNSW vector index. Not compatible with the sqlite3 CLI for schema-level access.
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or flags stated. Benchmark is first-party (tests/test_benchmark.c); the comparison SQLite benchmark harness lives in a separate author-controlled repo (hash-anu/sqllite-benchmark-kv), not independently reproduced. Author also claims comparisons vs LMDB and RocksDB in linked sibling repos, not verified here.

name: Bf-Tree
workload: Scan, write, and point-lookup workloads on small (~100 byte) records, comparing Bf-Tree's mini-page/buffer-pool design against RocksDB, generic B-Trees and LSM-Trees
claimed_speedup: 2.5x faster than RocksDB for scan operations, 6x faster than a B-Tree for write operations, 2x faster than both B-Trees and LSM-Trees for point lookup, for ~100-byte records (verbatim from repo README / VLDB 2024 abstract)
tradeoffs: Optimized specifically for modern SSDs where parallel random 4KB writes approach sequential throughput; heavily tuned for small (~100B) records -- large records perform like plain B-Trees/LSM-Trees; buffer-pool design is more complex than either baseline to implement correctly.
caveats: Author explicitly states the code is 'currently internal to Microsoft' and not public; this repo hosts only the paper, slides and poster (VLDB 2024). Peer-reviewed but unverifiable without the artifact, so capped at tier C per the no-code rule.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:b-plus-tree (via author XiangpengHao's repos)

name: indexset
workload: Single-threaded insert/contains/remove/get_index/full-traversal/range-scan and 12-thread concurrent (90/10 and 50/50 read/write mix) benchmarks over 100,000 existing 8-byte or 64-byte entries, Criterion median estimates at commit 7e3ac23
claimed_speedup: Concurrent indexset (cap 256) ~3.2x faster than a mutex-protected std::collections::BTreeMap under 50/50 64B contention (2.314ms vs 0.728ms, derived from page data); single-threaded full traversal ~2.5x faster (92.5us vs 37.3us for the 8B set case, verbatim); inserts 1.08-1.5x faster for small entries. std::BTreeMap/BTreeSet still wins plain get/remove/contains in the single-threaded case.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.97.0-nightly (ad3a598ca 2026-05-03); cargo bench via Criterion (default release profile; no extra flags itemized)
tradeoffs: Results are mixed rather than a uniform win: std::BTreeMap/BTreeSet is still faster for plain get/remove/contains, especially on larger 64-byte records; indexset wins full traversal, range scans, inserts, and concurrent-contention scenarios. Dense concurrent multimap workloads currently excluded pending an open issue.
caveats: Single-vendor benchmark (author's own Criterion suite on one machine); no independent reproduction; exact compiler flags beyond Criterion's default release profile not itemized.
